questions.q: According to this lesson's honest assessment, has QAOA been shown to outperform the best classical heuristics (simulated annealing, tabu search, specialized solvers) on industrially relevant problem sizes when benchmarked fairly?
options: Yes, but only for molecular ground-state problems, not combinatorial optimization
The question has never been investigated by any researcher
Yes, this has been conclusively and repeatedly demonstrated across all industrially relevant problem sizes
No -- it has found good approximate solutions on small, carefully studied instances, but has not demonstrated outperforming strong classical heuristics at relevant scale under fair benchmarking
questions.explain: The lesson states plainly that QAOA has shown good results on small instances, consistent with this course's own simulations, but has not been shown to beat strong classical heuristics at industrially relevant scale when benchmarked fairly -- some earlier favorable-looking comparisons turned out to use under-tuned classical baselines.

questions.q: What is the precise, research-literature meaning of 'quantum advantage'?
options: Any claim that a quantum algorithm has better theoretical scaling than a classical one, regardless of hardware demonstration
Evidence that quantum computers are generally more useful than classical computers for all tasks
A marketing term with no precise technical meaning at all
A demonstrated case where a quantum computer solves some problem faster than any known classical method can, on real hardware, for a real task
questions.explain: Quantum advantage has a precise meaning: an actual demonstrated case, on real hardware, of outperforming all known classical methods on some task -- it is not simply a theoretical scaling proof, which is why Lesson 18's proven-vs-demonstrated distinction matters here too.

questions.q: For which category of problems has quantum advantage been claimed and defended, according to this lesson, and what does the lesson say about optimization and finance?
options: Claimed broadly across combinatorial optimization, finance, and chemistry simultaneously
No quantum advantage has ever been claimed for any problem of any kind

Claimed for a small number of specific, deliberately non-practical sampling problems (like random circuit sampling); no such claim has been made or defended for combinatorial optimization or quantum finance
Claimed only for classical computing problems, never for anything quantum-related
questions.explain: The lesson is specific: quantum advantage has been claimed for narrow, non-practical sampling tasks like random circuit sampling, but not for optimization or finance -- a distinction the course insists on keeping precise rather than generalizing.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that problem structure matters more than raw problem size for determining whether a quantum method has a chance of competing?
options: Because highly structured problems are often solved extremely efficiently by specialized classical algorithms exploiting that structure, making them hardest to beat, while unstructured 'generic' hard instances put classical and quantum heuristics on more equal footing
Because problem size has no effect whatsoever on any optimization method's performance
Because classical computers cannot solve any structured problem regardless of size
Because quantum computers can only process structured problems, never unstructured ones
questions.explain: Specialized classical algorithms exploit symmetry, sparsity, or algebraic structure to solve certain large problems efficiently -- these structured cases are hardest for quantum methods to beat, whereas unstructured generic-hard instances are the more plausible (though still unproven) place to look for a quantum edge.

questions.q: What does the lesson identify as the things that would plausibly need to happen together for quantum optimization's competitive picture to shift?
options: Replacing QAOA and VQE entirely with classical-only algorithms
Nothing needs to change; the picture has already shifted in favor of quantum methods
Simply waiting for more research papers to be published, regardless of hardware or algorithmic improvements

Substantially larger/less noisy hardware approaching fault tolerance, better classical-optimizer techniques avoiding barren plateaus at scale, and identification of a specific problem structure with a provable or strong empirical quantum edge
questions.explain: The lesson names three plausible co-requirements: much better hardware (toward fault tolerance), improved classical optimization techniques that avoid barren plateaus at scale, and finding a specific problem structure with a genuine quantum edge -- with no guaranteed timeline for any of them.
